did_you_know.text: The chapter rejects the claim that the LORD permanently cast Israel away: the exile is described as the result of sins and transgressions, not as a divorce or sale carried out without cause.
The LORD displays his power through rhetorical questions: Is his hand too short to redeem and save? Immediately afterward, his power over the sea, the rivers, and the fish is described.
The ability to darken the heavens and clothe them in sackcloth is presented as a sign of the LORD’s control over nature and as an image of mourning and gloom.
The speaker says that the LORD has given him “the tongue of the learned”—the ability to speak a word to the weary—as well as an attentive ear to learn and listen.
The speaker emphasizes his faithfulness to his mission: after the LORD opened his ear, he did not rebel or turn back.

The speaker describes the suffering and humiliation he endured: being beaten on the back, having the hair of his cheeks pulled out, and being exposed to shame, insults, and spitting; despite this, he does not hide his face.
The speaker’s trust in the LORD is portrayed as the strength that enables him to endure shame: he sets his face “like flint” and knows that he will not be put to shame.
The speaker uses legal language to express his confidence: the LORD is near and vindicates him, so he challenges his opponents to appear before him.
The chapter addresses those who fear the LORD and encourages them to trust in the name of the LORD even when they walk in darkness and have no light.
The fire and sparks in the verse symbolically describe confidence that relies on one’s own strength; unlike those who trust in the LORD, such people may ultimately remain in distress.
